svg.text: Running a drip safely, and knowing when to stop it
The commonest fluid error on a ward is giving too much, too fast, to the wrong patient
The drop rate formula
volume in mL × drop factor
time in minutes
Adult giving set: 20 drops per mL
Blood set: 15 drops per mL
Paediatric burette: 60 drops per mL
1000 mL over 8 hours at 20 drops/mL = about 42 drops a minute
Signs you are giving too much
Breathlessness, and it started while the drip ran
Crackles at the lung bases
Rising pulse and rising respiratory rate
Neck veins full, new swelling of the legs
Frothy pink sputum — this is very late
Slow or stop the infusion, sit the patient up,
give oxygen, and call. Do not simply carry on.
Patients who overload easily
The very old and the very young
Heart failure of any cause
Kidney failure, or anyone passing little urine
Severe anaemia — the heart is already working hard
Severe acute malnutrition — a special case
In severe malnutrition the heart is weak and
standard rehydration kills. Use ReSoMal, slowly,
and stop if the pulse and breathing rise.
A rising pulse during rehydration means too much, not too little.
What to check before you start it
The prescription: fluid, volume, rate, additives
The bag: name, strength, expiry, clarity, seal
The patient: identity, allergy, weight
The site: no redness, swelling, pain or leak
The urine output since the last bag
And check the whole chart, not one line:
how much has this patient already had today?
Fluid is a drug. The bag has a dose and the dose can be exceeded.
